readerTitle: Why both shops stay open until 10 and both earn less
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 상점 두 곳, 부품 제조사 두 곳) + 개념의 유래 (1950년 RAND 연구, Tucker의 이름 붙이기) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 상대가 무엇을 하든 나에게 유리한 선택을 양쪽이 모두 하면, 둘 다 더 나빠질 수 있다. 문제는 사람의 탐욕이 아니라 보상 구조다.
misconception: 각자가 자기에게 가장 좋은 선택을 하면 결과도 모두에게 가장 좋다. 경쟁에서 지는 쪽은 판단을 잘못한 쪽이다.

sources.text: Flood, M. & Dresher, M. (1950). RAND Corporation 실험; Albert W. Tucker가 같은 해 '죄수' 이야기와 이름을 붙임
상점·제조사 수치는 모두 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 상점 수치 계산: 둘 다 7시 마감 시 각자 주 $3,000. 한쪽만 10시까지 영업 시 상대 고객 마진 $600을 가져오고 추가 인건비 $400 → 영업한 쪽 $3,000 + $600 − $400 = $3,200, 닫은 쪽 $3,000 − $600 = $2,400. 둘 다 영업 시 고객 이동 없음, 각자 인건비 $400 → $2,600. 상대가 닫으면 3,200 > 3,000, 상대가 열면 2,600 > 2,400이므로 '영업'이 항상 유리함을 확인했습니다.
개념의 유래: 1950년 RAND의 Merrill Flood와 Melvin Dresher가 게임을 만들고, Albert Tucker가 같은 해 강연에서 두 용의자 이야기로 설명하며 이름을 붙였다는 내용을 게시 전 Poundstone(1992) 등으로 다시 확인하세요.
경쟁사 간 가격 담합이 많은 나라에서 불법이라는 점은 일반적 사실로만 언급했습니다. 특정 국가의 법률 조언으로 읽히지 않도록 문구를 유지하세요.

cards.title: Why both shops stay open until 10 and both earn less
body: Two hardware stores face each other on a quiet street. Both used to close at 7. Now both stay open until 10.
The extra hours bring almost no new customers. Both owners pay staff to stand around. Neither owner is foolish. Each one made the smart move.

image.label: Two facing shops lit up late at night on an empty street
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 밤 10시, 텅 빈 거리 양쪽에 불 켜진 철물점 두 곳이 마주 봄. 각 가게 안에 지루한 표정의 직원 한 명씩. 벽시계는 9:55. 실제 브랜드 로고나 간판 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Should you stay open late?
body: You own one of the stores. You each earn about $3,000 a week. Staying open until 10 costs $400 a week in staff.
If only one store opens late, it wins $600 of the other's weekly business. You don't know what your rival will do.

options.feedback: You protect yourself whatever your rival does. But if they reason the same way, you both pay for empty evenings.

options.text: Close at 7 and hope your rival does too
options.feedback: This gives you both the best shared outcome. But if your rival opens late, you're the one who loses $600.

options.text: Wait and see what your rival does first
options.feedback: Waiting costs you sales if they open first. And once they do, you'll likely follow, so the end point is the same.

choice.afterReveal: Run the numbers on the next card: whatever your rival does, opening late earns you more. That's exactly the trap.

cards.title: Four possible weeks.
body: If your rival closes, opening earns you $3,200 instead of $3,000. If your rival opens, opening earns you $2,600 instead of $2,400. **Opening always wins for you.** Your rival sees the same math. So both open, and both drop from $3,000 to $2,600.

breakdown.label: You open, rival closes
breakdown.detail: You take $600 of their sales, pay $400 staff

cards.title: The prisoner's dilemma
body: A **prisoner's dilemma** is a situation where each side has a move that is better for itself no matter what the other does, yet when both make that move, both end up worse off.

The name comes from a 1950 story about two suspects questioned in separate rooms. Each is better off confessing, whatever the other does. So both confess, and both get longer sentences than if both had stayed silent.

image.label: Two-by-two grid with the bottom-right cell highlighted
image.brief: 2×2 보상표 인포그래픽. 가로 "Rival: Close / Open", 세로 "You: Close / Open". 네 칸에 $3,000/$3,000, $2,400/$3,200, $3,200/$2,400, $2,600/$2,600. 오른쪽 아래 칸이 강조되고, 왼쪽 위 칸에서 그쪽으로 미끄러지는 화살표.

cards.title: The same grid, in many costumes.
body: Look for two rivals and a move that helps one at the other's expense, but costs both when both make it.
list: **Discounts:** each cuts to steal customers, both lose margin
**Advertising:** each spends more to stay visible, the shares barely move
**Perks:** free delivery, longer returns, extra warranty
**Hiring:** each raises pay to poach staff from the other
cards.callout: Often the main winner is a third party: the customer, the ad seller, the worker.
cards.softwareNote: Two apps bidding on search ads for each other's brand names is a classic case. Each bid makes sense alone. Together they mostly raise the price the ad platform collects.

cards.title: Not every rivalry is a dilemma.
body: Check the numbers first. Sometimes the late hours do bring new customers, and both shops gain. That's just good business, not a trap.

Also, the obvious escape, agreeing prices or hours with a competitor, is illegal in many countries. The lawful exits change the grid itself: make your offer different, charge for the costly extra, or change what you compete on.
And rivals who meet every week play differently from strangers who meet once. That comes in a later lesson.

cards.title: Now it's two parts makers.
body: You and one rival make packaging for food factories. Your rival just promised free next-day delivery to every customer. Your trucks would need to run half-empty to match.
Customers say they like it, but few actually need it. What do you do?

options.text: Match free next-day delivery for everyone
options.feedback: You stop losing customers today. But you lock both firms into the costly corner of the grid, and the customers keep the savings.

options.text: Offer next-day delivery as a paid option, and keep standard delivery cheap
options.feedback: You change the payoffs: customers who need speed pay for it, and you don't fund empty trucks. You may lose a few accounts, but you leave the race.

options.text: Do nothing and hope the rival's costs force them to drop it
options.feedback: It might work, since the promise is costly for them too. But while you wait, customers who value speed drift away.

cards.title: When the smart move for each is bad for both, change the game.
body: A prisoner's dilemma isn't caused by bad people. It's caused by a payoff structure where each side's best move hurts both.
**Try it today:** list one thing you do mainly because a rival does it. Write what it costs you, and what would happen if you both stopped.
